desc:
Mice and holes sit on a number line. mice[i] is the position of the i-th mouse and holes[j] is the position of the j-th hole; both arrays have the same length n. Every mouse must run to a hole and every hole takes exactly one mouse. A mouse that runs from x to y travels |x - y|.

All mice run at the same time, so the rescue takes as long as the longest single run. Choose the assignment of mice to holes that makes this longest run as short as possible and return its length.

mice = [4, -4, 2], holes = [4, 0, 5]   -> 4
mice = [1, 5],     holes = [2, 6]      -> 1

In the first example the mouse at -4 must reach the hole at 0 (run 4), the mouse at 2 takes the hole at 4 (run 2) and the mouse at 4 takes the hole at 5 (run 1).
constraints: Several mice or holes may share a position
hints: Take two mice and two holes on the line. If the mice are in order a ≤ b and the holes in order c ≤ d, compare the assignments a→c, b→d and a→d, b→c. Which one has the smaller longest run?
Crossing paths never helps: swapping a crossing pair of assignments to a non-crossing one cannot increase the larger of the two distances.
Sort both arrays, match the i-th smallest mouse with the i-th smallest hole, and return the maximum of |mice[i] - holes[i]|.
editorial: Suppose mice a ≤ b are assigned to holes d and c with c ≤ d (a crossing pair). Re-assign them as a→c and b→d. On a line, each of the two new distances is at most the larger of the two old distances: every new run is contained in the span covered by the old ones, so the longest run of the pair does not grow. Repeating this removes all crossings without making the answer worse.

An assignment without crossings is exactly the sorted matching, so after sorting both arrays the answer is max |mice[i] - holes[i]|. Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time, O(n) extra space. A binary search over the answer with a feasibility check would also work but is unnecessary.
